reader.title: Ku-Klux warnings to Black residents of "Muncie county," Indiana
bases: The only report says employers of Black workers were warned to dismiss them and the Black residents were 'notified to leave' (A3); no violence beyond the warnings is reported.

One secondhand editorial paragraph (Minneapolis Tribune via the Bismarck Tribune) is the only report of warnings in 'Muncie county' (A3); other items describe Klan organizing and warnings elsewhere in Indiana but do not name Muncie (A2).

summary.text: The Ku-Klux warnings in "Muncie county," Indiana, were notices reported in August 1880 that told employers of Black workers in that county to dismiss them and told the Black residents themselves to leave.

The episode is known only from a short Republican editorial paragraph, first printed in the Minneapolis Tribune and reprinted in the Bismarck Tribune on August 13, which presented the warnings as part of the Democratic campaign in Indiana.

The report came during the 1880 presidential campaign, in which Hancock was the Democratic candidate and Garfield the Republican, when Republican papers charged that Indiana Democrats were organizing "Ku-Klux Klans" for the election.
An Ohio weekly carried that charge as a one-line news note on August 12, naming no place.
According to the Minneapolis Tribune, there were "a few negroes" in the county, and the people who employed them were "receiving regular ku-klux warnings to dismiss them and 'save trouble.'"
The Black residents themselves, the paragraph added, had "also been notified to leave."
It named no employer, worker or sender, gave no town or date, and did not say how the warnings were delivered or whether anyone left.
No report of arrests, an official response, or departures from the county appears in the coverage.
The item ran in the Bismarck Tribune among campaign paragraphs on its editorial page, under the heading "Hancock's Free Ballot."

The heading turned Hancock's promise of a free ballot against him, and the paragraph closed by calling the warnings "a part of the process by which the Hancock people intend to have a 'free ballot' in the Hoosier state."
Its interest was partisan: the Black residents appear only as evidence of Democratic methods, and no Indiana paper's account of the warnings was found.
No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

accounts.label: Minneapolis Tribune editorial paragraph (reprinted in the Bismarck Tribune)
accounts.gist: The ku-klux campaign in Indiana had begun: employers of the few Black people in 'Muncie county' were getting warnings to dismiss them, and the Black residents were told to leave, as part of the Democrats' plan for a 'free ballot'.

framing.detail: Headed 'Hancock's Free Ballot', the paragraph uses the warnings to mock Hancock's campaign promise and charges the 'Hancock people' with Klan methods in the 'Hoosier state' (A3).
A Republican Ohio weekly's news notes reported Indiana Democrats 'organizing Ku-Klux Klans' for the campaign, alongside items on Southern election violence (A2).

record_check.dossier: The paper prints "Muncie county"; no county by another name and no town are given.
No town named; the record's summary treats 'Muncie county' as a place, which is how the paper prints it.
Undated; on or before Aug. 13, 1880 (date of the reprint), originally in the Minneapolis Tribune on an unknown date.
'the ku-klux', tied by the paper to 'the Hancock people'; no one named.
Correct: one white mention, no Black-press coverage found.

record_check.record: Ku Klux warnings ... in Muncie county, Indiana ...
record_check.dossier: Accurate to the one source, but the warnings to employers, the 'save trouble' wording and the notices to leave closely match the Bluffton (Wells County) warnings reported Aug. 7 (A1); the Muncie paragraph may be a garbled secondhand version of that episode (record lean_1880-08_r2:g12).

sources.note: Editorial paragraph 'Hancock's Free Ballot', credited to the Minneapolis Tribune: employers of Black workers in 'Muncie county' receiving ku-klux warnings; Black residents told to leave. The only report of this episode.
quotes: The campaign of the ku-klux in Indiana has begun. There are a few negroes in Muncie county, of that state, it appears
the persons who give the blacks employment are receiving regular ku-klux warnings to dismiss them and "save trouble." The negroes themselves have also been notified to leave.
This is a part of the process by which tue Hancock people intend to have a "free ballot" in the Hoosier state.—Minneapolis Tribune.

set_aside: Bluffton, Ind. (Wells County) letter of Aug. 5: employers and a landlord warned by cards signed 'V. U. Q.' to get rid of Black workers and tenants and 'save trouble'; Black barber told to 'skip'. Same pattern and wording as the Muncie paragraph, but a different place.
'Political Points' quip quoting the Bluffton warning card ('get those niggers out of your building, and save trouble') attributed to 'Indiana Imitators of the K. K. K.'; no place named.
Cincinnati dispatch of Aug. 12: masked Kuklux attack on Joshua Mack near Columbus, Ind.; similar intimidation at Bluffton and Shelbyville. Muncie not named.
